ABSTRACT  
This work presents a novel Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) modeling and optimization frame -
work for the investment planning of large-scale hydrogen economy envelopes. The scope of the model includes 
the design, synthesis, and long-term capacity expansion of hydrogen supply chain networks (HSCN) that include 
hydrogen production, purification, storage, transportation, and distribution, subject to environmental sustain -
ability considerations. Production and carbon capture units are represented using surrogate models derived from 
rigorous simulations to capture important process non-linearities. This framework provides an optimal roadmap 
for the 10-year plan of hydrogen infrastructure development in the state of California, that demonstrates the 
important trade-offs between investment decisions, economic incentives, and regulatory carbon emissions con -
straints. It is shown that the development of the hydrogen production and distribution networks can be achieved 
over a 10-year horizon in an economically profitable way, while achieving a 90 % reduction in carbon emissions 
and satisfying all state regulatory mandates.   
1. Introduction 
The use of hydrogen as an energy carrier is being prompted nowa -
days by the growing interest in finding solutions that can contribute to 
the net zero emissions goal set by 2050. Hydrogen has a high-energy 
content, a low-carbon intensity, and it can be obtained from a wide 
range of low-carbon sources ( IEA, 2019 ). Current applications of 
hydrogen are mostly industrial, having only a very small footprint in the 
transportation area. Nevertheless, the hydrogen economy is expected to 
expand rapidly in the next decade. The report elaborated by Hydrogen 
Council (2021) , identified up to 35 new applications in transportation, 
heating, and power sectors out of which 22 will become 
cost-competitive by 2030. As a result, it is expected that hydrogen will 
make up an 18 % share of the total final energy consumption by 2050 
( International Renewable Energy Agency IRENA, 2019 ). In this new 
context, decisions makers will invest in solutions that address the future 
challenges related to the entire hydrogen supply chain including pro -
duction, storage, transportation, and end-use cases. 
Fossil fuels are the primary sources of hydrogen with a 79 % share of 
the global production. Steam methane reforming (SMR) and coal 
gasification are currently the most common production technologies. 
The production of hydrogen in 2020 resulted in 900 Mt of CO
2 
emis -
sions, equivalent to the emissions of Indonesia and the United Kingdom 
combined ( IEA, 2021 ). Further efforts are needed to offer cost-effective 
and cleaner alternatives to produce hydrogen. In this context, some 
countries in North America and Europe have been deploying projects 
accounting for carbon capture technologies in hydrogen production ( Yu 
et al., 2021 ). 
Alternative routes have also been developed including the use of 
renewable resources as raw materials with no-direct emissions gener -
ated. In this respect, electrolysis is nowadays the most promising of 
those technologies. Increasingly, hydrogen producers are leading pro -
jects to deploy assets incorporating renewables-based electrolysis to 
produce hydrogen with minimal carbon footprint. Some examples are 
the projects led by Shell (2022) ; ( Rephyne, 2021 ), Iberdrola (2022) and 
Linde (2022) . Even more, Guerras et al. (2019) reported that electrolysis 
could produce hydrogen at competitive prices against the fuel cost of 
gasoline vehicles when dynamic pricing for electricity is used in some 
states of the US. On the other hand, hydrogen can also be obtained from 
biomass through a gasification process; however, the production costs 
are still higher when compared with conventional process ( Davis and

Although the production cost yielded twice the one of conventional 
SMR, the authors claimed that a reduction of 65 % of carbon emissions 
can be reached. 
A more diversified hydrogen economy will also include specialized 
applications requiring different purity standards. Du et al. (2021) report 
that up to three purity grades of hydrogen are being used in the trans -
portation sector ranging from pure (99.9 %) to ultra-pure (99.999 %). 
Under this scheme, the purity costs not only will depend on the tech -
nology used to produce hydrogen but also on its final application. This 
item was addressed by Wickham et al. (2022) who concluded that the 
purity cost could represent as much as 30 % of the total discounted in -
vestment cost of a hydrogen supply chain designed for UK. The authors 
proposed the use of correlations to estimate the purification cost based 
on the initial and final hydrogen purity. The hydrogen purity obtained 
from a steam methane process was assumed to be 95 %. Therefore, 
additional purification is needed so that hydrogen can be sent to the 
fueling stations. In this work, we present an approach that addresses two 
distinct purification steps. The first one is calculated based on the 
product distribution obtained from each type of technology and the 
second is used to adjust the purity to the transportation specifications 
when required. 
Modeling hydrogen production represents only a fraction of the 
whole supply chain. The complete Hydrogen Supply Chain Network 
(HSCN) also includes hydrogen transportation and storage. Hydrogen 
requires high transportation and storage volumes because of its low 
volumetric energy density (68 % lower than natural gas), which in -
creases the final cost. The best choice partially relies on the scale of 
HSCN. For instance, Yang and Ogden (2007) reported that when an 
amount lower than 14 MT/day is transported over a short distance, the 
use of gas trucks becomes the most economical option. For longer dis -
tances, the use of liquid hydrogen trucks and pipelines is preferred. 
Other solutions in this respect consider the conversion of hydrogen into 
compounds with higher volumetric energy density, i.e., ammonia and 
liquid organic carriers ( Hydrogen Council, 2021 ; Chyoda Corporation, 
2020 ) and blending it into natural gas pipelines ( Melania et al. 2013 ; 
Penchev et al., 2022 ). One example of the latter is the HyNTS project led 
by the National Grid in UK, which aims at the full conversion of the gas 
transmission system to transport hydrogen. ( Sadler et al., 2016 ; Na -
tional Grid, 2021 ). The challenge for both options is that the H

the low hydrogen diffusion in water, the depleted hydrocarbon deposits 
and aquifers would be preferred over the salt caverns, which are usually 
dry structures. A large amount of hydrogen can be stored using lique -

boil-off rates are drawbacks for long-term storage ( Barthelemy et al., 
2017 ). 
The optimal design of a HSCN has been traditionally addressed by 
formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that 
includes a superstructure representation of the alternative production, 
storage, transmission, as well as primary and secondary distribution 
modes and technologies. The work by Almansoori and Shah (2006) 
presented a modeling framework to include production, transport, and 
storage of hydrogen with no explicit time consideration. This model was 
then extended in Almansoori and Shah (2009) to a multi-period 
approach by adding hydrogen demand variations, availability of en -
ergy resources, capacity expansion, fueling stations, and local and 
regional transfers. Guill ´en-Gonz ´albez et al. (2010) addressed the prob -
lem using a multi-objective optimization approach where life cycle 
assessment (LCA) principles were used to build a second objective 
function aimed at reducing the environmental impact of the HSCN. A 
similar approach was used by Sabio et al. (2010) who considered the 
financial risk, driven by uncertain operating cost, as a third objective 
function. Agnolucci et al. (2013) incorporated spatially detailed sce -
narios for hydrogen demand, which are estimated using socioeconomic 
data including access to cars, education, commuting distance, and 
household income. The model also includes decisions on the infra -
structure needed for the final disposition of CO
2 
when carbon capture 
and storage (CCS) is selected. Reu ß et al. (2019a) also addressed the 
spatial distribution of demand with a special focus on hydrogen trans -
mission and distribution blocks. As part of the transportation modes 
considered, the model incorporated the use of hydrogen carriers such as 
liquid organics (LOC). The authors concluded that under restrictive 
scenarios of CO
2 
emissions, the LOCs were not competitive compared to 
conventional transports because of the heat required to conduct the 
dehydrogenation step at the fueling station. Nunes et al. (2015) , 
formulated a stochastic model to account for the uncertainty of 
hydrogen demand over time. First-stage decisions were investments in 
production plants and storage facilities, while second-stage decisions 
were transportation contracts and supply chain operation logistics. 
Other examples of models considering uncertainty include the ones 
developed by Almansoori and Shah (2012) and Bique et al. (2021) . 
Despite the extend of the cited research, none of the models 
mentioned above capture the intermittent behavior of renewables over 
time, nor do they consider the interactions of the power grid with 
hydrogen production. Both items are of interest as the share of green 
hydrogen is expected to increase. To address this limitation, Samsatli 
et al. (2016) proposed a model that considers operational and design 
decisions of hydrogen supply chains interacting with wind farms. Under 
this scheme, energy can be transmitted as electricity and hydrogen. The 
model includes the characterization of the hourly variability of wind 
velocity, and the spatial-temporal characterization of hydrogen demand 
using Geographic Information Systems (GIS). This work was extended 
by Samsatli and Samsatli (2019) to include household heating demand 
in the UK. Here hydrogen is sent directly to domestic combined 
heat-power plants or to hydrogen boilers, which generate high-grade 
heat used in district heating. Results showed that over 20 % of heat 
could be covered by hydrogen. He et al. (2021) modeled the interactions 
with the grid assuming distinct scenarios of power production mix under 
different carbon prices. The authors conclude that a higher carbon price 
leads to a higher share of electrolysis in hydrogen production. The dy -
namics of storage and transmission systems were also affected by the 
electricity price. During the off-peak electricity price periods and low 
demands for hydrogen, the system increases the hydrogen stored that is 
then released during the high hydrogen demand periods. Some authors 
have considered the rigorous modeling of pipeline flows ( Reuss et al. 
2019b ) and hydrogen secondary purification ( Wickham et al., 2022 ). 
All the publications reviewed so far formulated the HSCN optimi -
zation problem as a MILP, assuming linear relations of hydrogen pro -
duction and utility consumption. Moreover, technologies integrating 
carbon capture were often modeled as single entities, ignoring impor -
tant design and operating constraints. A more accurate representation of 
hydrogen production technologies is necessary not only to improve the 
quality of the optimal solutions, but to also provide a better under -
standing of the effects of these operating variables on the hydrogen 
supply chain. It is, therefore, the main objective of this work to present a 
framework to incorporate the rigorous modeling of hydrogen produc -
tion technologies as part of a hydrogen strategic investment planning 
and supply chain optimization model. The problem is formulated as a 
multi-period MINLP and it is used to select the best technologies to 
produce, store, and transport hydrogen across large geographic enve -
lopes and over extensive timeframes. In the temporal dimension, the 
model aims to produce an optimal long-term investment strategy to 
deploy and expand hydrogen production, storage, and primary distri -
bution capacity. Purity requirements are very important and are 
addressed by considering two hydrogen purities: low (95 %) used by the 
industrial sector, and high (99.9 % + ) used by the transportation sector. 
The contributions of this work are summarized below:  
1 We use nonlinear reduced order models (ROMs) to better represent 
the hydrogen production and carbon capture processes for the 
optimal design of a Hydrogen Supply Chain Network (HSCN).  
2 We model the process of carbon capture as a separate modeling 
construct using ROMs that account for individual mass balances for 
flue gas components and solvents.  
3 We consider the production and distribution of hydrogen with 
different purity specifications for use in both transportation and/or 
industrial processes. The purification cost is a function of the product 
distribution, and it is obtained for each type of technology and the 
final use of hydrogen. 
4 We finally present a detailed case study for the entire state of Cali -
fornia that accounts for all the state ’ s decarbonization mandates and 
optimally incorporates the time-varying emissions targets over a ten- 
year horizon ( CARB, 2018 ). 
The rest of the work is organized as follows. First, we present an 
overall description of the network topology as a superstructure model 
representation used to design the HSCN. Then, we describe the meth -
odology used to build ROMs and to formulate of the overall model. 
Section 4 highlights the modeling and optimization aspects of this work 
using the California hydrogen economy plan as a case study. Section 5 
discusses some aspects of the ROMs formulated and the results obtained 
from the case study. Finally, we summarize our conclusions in Section 6 . 
2. Superstructure description 
The proposed problem involves selecting the best long-term config -
uration of a hydrogen supply chain that maximizes profitability while 
meeting projected hydrogen demand and complying with carbon 
emission regulatory constraints. The model must select the best location 
and technologies to produce, store, and transport hydrogen with 
different modes and purities. Fig. 1a provides a high-level description of 
the five key modeling envelopes that constitute the entire hydrogen 
supply chain network. Fig. 1b provides a more detailed picture of the 
superstructure modeling approach for the hydrogen supply chain, 
including the specific process unit operations and the specific network 
interconnection among the six modeling blocks: primary hydrogen 
production facilities, low and high purification facilities, phase condi -
tioning (i.e., compression and liquefaction), storage, transmission, and 
delivery. Here, we considered coal gasification (with and without car -
bon capture), steam methane reforming (with and without carbon cap -
ture), biomass gasification (with and without carbon capture), and

We assumed that the area of study can be divided into smaller zones 
based on the customer locations. The customers in each zone are clus -
tered into two categories based on the hydrogen final use: automotive or 
industrial. For that purpose, we assumed two qualities of hydrogen to be 
supplied, i.e., low (used by the industrial sector) and high purity 
(consumed by the automotive sector). The former is obtained from the 
low purification block with 95 % as purity, while the latter requires an 
extra purification step to meet the specifications of fuel cell electric 
vehicles, i.e., 99.9 %. 
Low- and high-purity hydrogen is sent to the conditioning section, 
where it is compressed or liquified depending on its final disposition. For 
instance, hydrogen is compressed to 350 bars when stored as com -
pressed gas, to 180 bars when transferred using gas trucks, and 100 bars 
when transferred using pipelines or liquefied when stored and trans -
ported as a liquid. After being conditioned, hydrogen is transferred 
(either imported or exported) to other zones by using gas and liquid 
trucks or pipelines. It is worth mentioning that the conditioning, storage, 
and transportation sections are modeled separately for both types of 
hydrogen, avoiding blending between the two product qualities. The 
transferred hydrogen can be stored, sent directly to the customer (in case 
of low purity hydrogen), or, in case of high purity hydrogen, sent to the

3. Model description 
In this section, we present the methodology followed to construct 
reduced order models. Then, in Section 3.2 , the main modeling equa -
tions and assumptions are described. 
3.1. Methodology to develop a reduced order model 
Reduced order models (ROMs) were constructed aimed at capturing 
the nonlinear behavior of the SMR and carbon capture technologies 
respectively. The proposed approach is presented in Fig. 2 and is 
described as follows. First, the main units of the process are modeled in 
Aspen HYSYS ® ( Aspen Technology, 2023a ) based on rigorous first 
principles equations. Here, the overall performance of the process is 
studied through sensitivity analyses of the key operating variables. 
Then, multiple scenarios for those operating variables are created in 
Aspen multi-case ® ( Aspen Technology, 2023b ) with the aim to solve 
multiple simulations in parallel and generate enough data to construct 
the ROM. This framework also requires the selection of independent and 
dependent variables. In this work, the independent variables were 
related with the main input streams of the process (i.e., Feedstock 
flowrate) and some operating variables (i.e., temperature and pressure). 
On the other hand, the dependent variables include the output streams 
of the process (i.e., products flowrate) and utilities consumption. A 
detailed description is shown in the next section. Once generated, the 
data is exported as a . Json file to Aspen AI model builder ® (AIMB). The 
latter utilizes artificial intelligence principles to correlate the data gotten 
from the simulations and construct non-linear relationships (also called 
ROMs) between independent and dependent variables ( Aspen Tech -
nology, 2023c ). In this work, we used the linear regression method that 
incorporates polynomial terms. Once created, the ROM is deployed as 
an.XLP file containing the matrix structure and non-linear coefficient 
information that can be consumed by the Aspen technology proprietary 
MINLP solver called Aspen XSLP ® ( Varvarezos, 2008 ; Khor and Var -
varezos, 2017 ). Finally, the optimization problem is solved in Aspen 
PIMS-AO ® , as well as Aspen Unified PIMS ® , the planning optimization 
and modeling frameworks most widely used in the petroleum and 
petrochemical industry to solve large MINLP problems including 
multi-period and multi-plant models ( Aspen Technology, 2023d , 
2023e ). 
3.1.1. Steam methane reforming 
The modeling of this section was developed as a reduced-order 
model derived from rigorous simulation data using Aspen HYSYS 
( Aspen Technology, 2023a ). The process consists of three sections: 
reformer reactor, high-and low-temperature water gas shift (WGS) re -
actors, and tail gas recycling and is described as follows. Natural gas and 
steam are sent to the reformer reactor and converted into syngas (a 
mixture of CO, CO
2

shift reactors where the carbon monoxide and the remaining methane 
are converted into hydrogen plus CO
2

separation unit from which two streams are obtained: hydrogen and the 
remaining tail gasses. The tail gasses are sent to a combustion chamber 
to produce the steam required by the reformer reactor.

4. Case study 
The model presented here was used to optimize the strategic plan -
ning investment for developing the hydrogen supply chain in the state of 
California. One hydrogen consumer in California is the transportation 
sector. According to the California Air Resources Board ( CARB, 2021 ), 
the state of California currently has 67 fueling stations installed, with an 
average capacity of 250 kg/day, that supply the hydrogen required by 
over 10,000 fuel-cell electric vehicles (FCEV). As part of the same efforts 
to decarbonize the sector, the current legislation (Assembly Bill 32, 
2006), mandates the decrease of carbon emissions to the 1990 ′ s level 
and increase the use of renewables from 50 % to 100 % to produce 
energy by the end of this decade ( CARB, 2018 ). The other large 
hydrogen consumer in the state, is the refinery sector with a total de -
mand of 2100 Mt/day, which is supplied on-site or by gas companies 
through SMR process. In this work, we use the proposed approach to 
supply the demand of both customers assuming they require different 
qualities of hydrogen, i.e., high-purity hydrogen for fueling stations and 
low-purity for refineries. 
For modeling purposes, we have lumped the hydrogen demand in 
four zones that roughly correspond to the cities having the largest ca -
pacity of fueling stations, namely, San Francisco, Sacramento, San 
Diego, and Los Angeles (see Fig. 4 a and b, AFDC, 2022 ). Installation of 
storage was not included because of the coarse time discretization used. 
We also considered to supply the hydrogen required by the refineries 
located at those cities based on information taken from Gilani and 
Sanchez (2020) . The estimated hydrogen demand for each zone is shown 
in Table S10. Here, we considered a time horizon of ten years from 2023 
to 2032. Carbon emissions for SMR, coal, and biomass gasification were 
estimated as the CO

5. Results 
In this section, a brief discussion on the ROMs obtained for the SMR 
and CCU processes is presented. Then, we discuss the hydrogen supply 
chain design and capacity deployment for the case study from two 
perspectives. First, we solve the problem with no restrictions on the 
carbon emission. Later, a second solution is presented including the 
carbon emission constraints inscribed in the legislation of the state of 
California. 
5.1. Discussion on the reduced order models 
As discussed, ROMs for steam methane reforming and carbon cap -
ture were developed through AI model builder. They consist of poly -
nomial functions taking care of relevant variables that might affect the 
performance of the process. In this section, we discussed the non-liner 
behavior of the process which is revealed in the coefficients and parity 
plots. 
5.1.1. Steam methane reformer process 
Fig. 5 shows the coefficient plots for the dependent variables studied 
in the SMR process. Note that the y-axis indicates the polynomial terms 
included in the ROM, while the x-axis shows the coefficient value of each 
term. Here, one can observe that the linear terms are predominant in the 
ROMs and influenced by the total feed variable (SSMRINS). The latter 
captures all the input streams of the process. Namely, natural gas as 
feedstock, and the air and water used to produce steam. Then, we added 
natural gas and steam inputs as two separate variables aiming at 
studying their individual contribution. Overall, the natural gas feed 
(SSMRNGG) accounts for the most predominant effect over the products 
flowrates. On the other hand, the non-linearities of the process are 
mainly triggered by the reformer temperature (SSMRTEM) appearing in 
the quadratic and bilinear terms. The coefficient plots show that a 
temperature increase favors the hydrogen production, but it also leads to 
higher CO
2 
emissions. The last statement makes sense since most of the 
SMR and WGS reactions are endothermic. Therefore, a major decision of 
the model is to find the trade-off between these two conflicting vari -
ables. Unlike reformer temperature, reformer pressure does not show a 
significant effect on the dependent variables studied.

correspond with the CO

gas stream and the streams coming from the flash drums. In this case, the 
following remarks can be extracted from the coefficient plots shown in

6. Conclusions 
A mixed-integer non-linear model was developed for the strategic 
investment planning related to the design and long-term capacity 
expansion of hydrogen supply chains. The best configuration of the 
HSCN is determined through a superstructure that maximizes the prof -
itability of the network, while meeting the projected hydrogen demand. 
It includes six blocks: production, purification, conditioning, storage, 
transport, and delivery. We also presented a methodology to build 
reduced order models aimed at capturing the business-important non- 
linearities of the technologies involved in the production block. The 
methodology uses data extracted from rigorous simulations models to 
construct non-linear relationships between the dependent and inde -
pendent variables. In this respect, results also showed that the necessity 
of including non-linearities for the SMR is triggered by the temperature 
of the reformer reactor. Coefficient plots revealed that a temperature 
increase favors the hydrogen production, but it also leads to higher CO
2 
emissions. As for the carbon capture process, we observed that the sol -
vent recovery step was mainly affected by the total amount of nitrogen 
content and the solvent flowrate required to absorb CO
2. 
An increase in 
the flowrate of solvent and nitrogen leads to a decrease in the total 
amount of CO
2 
obtained in the flash drums used to recover the solvent. 
These models were included in the HSCN model used to solve a case 
study aimed at the development of hydrogen infrastructure for the state 
of California. The technoeconomic analysis showed that the use of SMR 
and electrolysis were the preferred technologies to produce hydrogen. In 
particular, SMR plants are used to satisfy the demand for low-purity 
hydrogen, while electrolysis plants supply the high-purity hydrogen 
for transportation. The optimal solution also calls for liquid trucks to 
transfer hydrogen between the zones and gas trucks for smaller quan -
tities and short distances. In this respect, low-purity hydrogen was 
mainly transferred using compressed hydrogen gas trucks, while high- 
purity hydrogen transportation utilized primarily liquid hydrogen 
trucks. The increasing CO
2 
emissions constraints strongly influenced the 
decisions on how and when the infrastructure was deployed. Results 
showed that the expansion of SMR was conducted with the installation 
of carbon units. As the CO
2 
constraint became more restrictive, the ca -
pacity expansion of electrolysis was favored over SMR, largely because 
of the expected increase of renewable share in power grid by the end of 
the decade. The total number of fueling stations capacity in periods 
2023 – 2029 was similar to the one projected by the California energy 
commission. Moreover, it was also shown that the expansion of elec -
trolysis prompted the installation of new fueling stations by 2032. Under 
the latter scheme, the optimizer was able to reduce the carbon emissions 
at the last period by 90 % with respect to the base case. Results also 
showed that when 1 % of loss in profitability is allowed, the total carbon 
emissions can be reduced by 10.8 %. As for the carbon tax, optimization 
results revealed that even with a modest penalty, carbon emissions can 
be reduced by 11 % and up to 20 % compared to a 73 % carbon 
reduction resulting from the regulatory framework in place and without 
any explicit carbon tax (as can be seen in Table 2 ). 
Finally, it is worth noting, that the optimal total investment cost 
results are consistent with the stated estimates from the state of Cali -
fornia. In fact, the optimal policy approach, developed here, yields a 
lower total investment ($6.9B versus $8B allocation, ( GO-Biz, 2022 )), 
while satisfying all the projected hydrogen demands and the emission 
constraints from the underlying regulatory framework. Furthermore, 
this investment not only reduces emissions (by 90 % in 2032), but it is 
also cash-flow positive with a discounted cash flow of $1.4B. We expect 
that such modeling and optimization frameworks will greatly assist the 
accelerated and economical achievement of worldwide emission 
reduction targets set by both corporate and government entities.
